nameStory: The Four-eyed Butterflyfish gets its name from the distinctive dark eyespots on each side of its body near the tail, giving it the appearance of having four eyes total. These false eyes are thought to confuse predators about which end is the head, helping the fish escape danger by swimming away in an unexpected direction.
description: The Four-eyed Butterflyfish is a stunning tropical fish with a compressed, disc-like body that's pale yellow to white with intricate patterns. True to its name, it displays prominent dark eyespots near its tail fin, along with a dark band running through its actual eye. This small but eye-catching fish typically grows to about 6 inches long and is known for its graceful, fluttering swimming style that resembles a butterfly's flight.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Two dark eyespots near the tail fin on each side of the body, with a pale yellow to white base color and darker vertical lines or bands across the body

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deeply compressed, almost circular body that feels thin and delicate, like a dinner plate turned sideways

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Rounded dorsal and anal fins that extend far back along the body, with soft rays that feel flexible to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish reaching about 6 inches in length, roughly the size of your hand from wrist to fingertips

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, pointed mouth positioned at the front tip of the snout, perfect for picking at small prey in crevices

habitat: In New England waters, Four-eyed Butterflyfish are rare visitors typically found in warmer coastal areas, especially around rocky reefs, jetties, and artificial structures in shallow to moderate depths. They prefer areas with plenty of hiding spots and feeding opportunities among rocks and coral-like growth. These tropical fish are most likely encountered during warmer months when Gulf Stream currents may carry them northward.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in New England waters during spring as water temperatures are still too cool for these tropical visitors.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to spot them in New England as warming waters and Gulf Stream currents may bring individuals northward to our coastal areas.
seasonality.fall: Occasional sightings possible in early fall before water temperatures drop, though they cannot survive the approaching winter.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters due to cold temperatures that are lethal to these tropical fish.

funFact: Four-eyed Butterflyfish are actually terrible at surviving New England winters - they're tropical fish that occasionally ride the Gulf Stream north like hitchhikers, but they can't make the return trip and will die when water temperatures drop below about 68°F, making every New England sighting a rare treat!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the Spotfin Butterflyfish, but the Four-eyed has two distinct dark eyespots near the tail while the Spotfin has a dark spot on its dorsal fin instead. Remember: 'Four eyes near the tail, not a spot on the sail.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting they live in New England, Four-eyed Butterflyfish are actually tropical visitors that represent the northern edge of their range here. The 9 recorded observations in New England represent rare sightings of individuals carried north by ocean currents, not an established population.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Spotfin Butterflyfish, the Four-eyed has the distinctive twin eyespots near its tail fin, while the Spotfin lacks these rear eyespots but has a prominent dark spot on its dorsal fin. Both share the same compressed body shape and pale coloration, but the eyespot pattern is the key difference between these two butterflyfish species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its closest relative, the four-eyed butterflyfish, the spotfin has its signature spot on the top dorsal fin rather than prominent eyespots on the body sides.
